title: Possessors: minulla, sinulla, hänellä, meillä, teillä, heillä
summary: Finnish says who has something with a possessor form ending in -lla or -llä. This is called the adessive owner form: it names the person who has the thing.
objectives: Choose minulla, sinulla, hänellä, meillä, teillä, or heillä for the person who has something.
Recognise the pattern, then produce it with the supporting words shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Finnish says who has something with a possessor form ending in -lla or -llä. This is called the adessive owner form: it names the person who has the thing.
Learn the six pronoun forms as a table rather than adding an ending directly to minä or sinä.
Hänellä can refer to a man or a woman. Sinulla addresses one person; teillä addresses a group in these tasks. Teillä can also address one person politely when that context is stated.
keyPoints: Possessors: minulla, sinulla, hänellä, meillä, teillä, heillä

steps: Start from minä (“I”) and learn its owner form minulla. Do not attach -lla directly to minä.
The shown on supplies “have” in this possession pattern.
pallo names one ball; put it after on.
Sinä (“you”, one person) becomes sinulla. This differs from the group form teillä.
The shown on supplies “have” in this possession pattern.
kirja names one book; put it after on.
Hän (“he” or “she”) has the owner form hänellä. Gender does not change that Finnish form.
The shown on supplies “has” in this possession pattern.
koira names one dog; put it after on.
Me (“we”) becomes meillä: several owners can have one thing.
The shown on supplies “have” in this possession pattern.
auto names one car; put it after on.
Te (“you”, a group here) becomes teillä. Use sinulla when speaking to one person in these tasks.
The shown on supplies “have” in this possession pattern.
peli names one game; put it after on.
He (“they”) becomes heillä. Keep it distinct from singular hänellä.
The shown on supplies “have” in this possession pattern.
kynä names one pen; put it after on.
Reuse minulla for the same owner with a different thing; the noun does not change the owner form.
The shown on supplies “have” in this possession pattern.
kissa names one cat; put it after on.
Reuse meillä for a group of owners; its -llä is part of the learned pronoun form.
The shown on supplies “have” in this possession pattern.
tyyny names one pillow; put it after on.

commonMistakes: Use minulla for “I have”, rather than the subject pronoun minä. Learn the pronoun forms as a table; minä + -lla does not give minulla.
Use sinulla for one person addressed as “you” and teillä for a group.
Keep hänellä (“he/she as owner”) distinct from heillä (“they as owner”); Finnish does not change hänellä for gender.

practiceExercises.prompt: Optional practice: Write the possessor form for “They have a ball.” Frame: “___ on pallo.” Use pallo (“a ball”) and on (“have/has”).
practiceExercises.explanation: Use heillä, the possession form of he. The owner comes before fixed on.
practiceExercises.misconceptionCategory: Personal possessor forms: form or meaning confused

sentenceExplanation.pattern: possessor + fixed on + one thing in its basic singular form

parts.role: possessor: the person who has the thing
parts.formation: he has the learned possession form heillä; its -lla/-llä ending marks the possessor. Learn this pronoun form as a whole.
Olla means “to be”; possession uses its fixed on form with every owner, including we and they.
pallo stays in its basic singular form: one ball.

optionFeedback.minulla: Use minulla, the possession form of minä. The owner comes before fixed on.
optionFeedback.sinulla: sinulla identifies you as the owner; the requested owner is I.
optionFeedback.hänellä: hänellä identifies he as the owner; the requested owner is I.
optionFeedback.meillä: meillä identifies we as the owner; the requested owner is I.
optionFeedback.teillä: teillä identifies you as the owner; the requested owner is I.
optionFeedback.heillä: heillä identifies they as the owner; the requested owner is I.
